q1: SELECT DISTINCT T2.label FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.element != 'sn'
q2: SELECT label FROM molecule WHERE molecule_id NOT IN (SELECT molecule_id FROM atom WHERE element = 'sn')
explanation: Q1 returns labels of molecules that have at least one non-'sn' atom. Q2 returns labels of molecules that have no 'sn' atoms at all (and also includes molecules with no atoms); with NOT IN it can also be affected by NULLs. Thus, molecules that have both 'sn' and non-'sn' atoms are included by Q1 but excluded by Q2.
counterexample_dsp: Two molecules: m1 has atoms 'sn' and 'c'; m2 has no atoms. Q1 returns m1 (has a non-'sn' atom). Q2 returns m2 (m1 is excluded because it has an 'sn' atom).

q2: SELECT T1.atom_id, T1.atom_id2 FROM connected AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id WHERE T2.bond_type = '#'

q1: SELECT CAST(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN T1.element <> 'f' THEN T2.molecule_id ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(DISTINCT T2.molecule_id) FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+'
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.element != 'F' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T1.molecule_id) FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN atom AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.label = '+'
explanation: Q1 computes the percentage of '+' molecules that have at least one atom whose element is not 'f' (molecule-level, COUNT DISTINCT molecules). Q2 computes the percentage of atoms (within '+' molecules) whose element is not 'F' (atom-level, SUM over atoms). They differ in aggregation grain and even compare to different literals ('f' vs 'F'), so they are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: One '+' molecule with two atoms: one with element 'F' and one with element 'Cl'. Q1 counts the molecule as having a non-'f' atom, yielding 100%. Q2 counts 1 of 2 atoms as not 'F', yielding 50%.

q1: SELECT CAST(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN T2.label = '+' THEN T2.molecule_id ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(DISTINCT T2.molecule_id) FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id INNER JOIN bond AS T3 ON T2.molecule_id = T3.molecule_id WHERE T3.bond_type = '#'
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.bond_type = '#' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T2.bond_id) FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.label = '+'
explanation: Q1 computes the percentage of molecules (that have at least one atom and at least one '#' bond) whose label is '+'. Q2 computes the percentage of bonds that are '#' among '+'-labeled molecules. They aggregate on different grains (molecules vs bonds) and apply different filters, so they are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Three molecules: M1 labeled '+', with two atoms and bonds {#, -}; M2 labeled '-', with one atom and bond {#}; M3 labeled '+', with one atom and bond {-}. Q1 sees molecules with '#' bonds (M1, M2) and returns 1/2=50% '+'; Q2 considers bonds of '+' molecules (M1, M3) and returns 1/3≈33.33% '#'.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T.element FROM atom AS T WHERE T.molecule_id = 'TR000' ORDER BY T.element LIMIT 3
q2: SELECT element FROM atom WHERE molecule_id = 'TR000' ORDER BY element ASC LIMIT 3
explanation: Q1 returns up to 3 distinct element values for molecule TR000, while Q2 returns the first 3 rows (allowing duplicates) ordered by element. They differ when TR000 has duplicate elements.
counterexample_dsp: If molecule TR000 has atoms with duplicate elements (e.g., two Cs, one H, one O), Q1 yields C,H,O while Q2 yields C,C,H.

q1: SELECT SUBSTR(T.bond_id, 1, 7) AS atom_id1 , T.molecule_id || SUBSTR(T.bond_id, 8, 2) AS atom_id2 FROM bond AS T WHERE T.molecule_id = 'TR001' AND T.bond_id = 'TR001_2_6'
q2: SELECT T1.atom_id, T1.atom_id2 FROM connected AS T1 INNER JOIN atom AS T2 ON T1.atom_id = T2.atom_id INNER JOIN bond AS T3 ON T1.bond_id = T3.bond_id WHERE T3.molecule_id = 'TR001' AND T3.bond_id = 'TR001_2_6'
explanation: Q1 fabricates two atom ids by string-splitting/concatenating the bond_id and molecule_id, independent of any CONNECTED/ATOM data. Q2 returns the actual atom pairs recorded in CONNECTED for that bond (and filters by the bond’s molecule). These are different logics; results can differ in both content and cardinality.
counterexample_dsp: Create the bond TR001_2_6 in molecule TR001, and record in CONNECTED that it links atoms TR001_3 and TR001_5. Q1 will compute (TR001_2, TR001_6) from the bond_id string, while Q2 will return the actual pair (TR001_3, TR001_5).

q1: SELECT COUNT(CASE WHEN T.label = '+' THEN T.molecule_id ELSE NULL END) - COUNT(CASE WHEN T.label = '-' THEN T.molecule_id ELSE NULL END) AS diff_car_notcar FROM molecule t
q2: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN label = '+' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) - SUM(CASE WHEN label = '-' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DIFFERENCE FROM molecule
explanation: Both compute (# of '+' rows) minus (# of '-' rows). They differ when the table is empty: COUNT(...) yields 0 while SUM(...) yields NULL, so Q1 returns 0 and Q2 returns NULL.
counterexample_dsp: Empty table: with no rows in MOLECULE, Q1 = 0−0 = 0, Q2 = NULL−NULL = NULL.

q1: SELECT T.atom_id FROM connected AS T WHERE T.bond_id = 'TR000_2_5'
q2: SELECT T1.atom_id, T1.atom_id2 FROM connected AS T1 WHERE T1.bond_id = 'TR_000_2_5'
explanation: Not equivalent: Q1 filters on bond_id = 'TR000_2_5' and returns only atom_id; Q2 filters on bond_id = 'TR_000_2_5' (different literal) and returns both atom_id and atom_id2.
counterexample_dsp: Create one molecule, four atoms, two bonds with IDs 'TR000_2_5' and 'TR_000_2_5', and two CONNECTED rows using different atom pairs for each bond. Q1 returns A1; Q2 returns (A3, A4).

q1: SELECT T.bond_id FROM connected AS T WHERE T.atom_id2 = 'TR000_2'
q2: SELECT bond_id FROM connected WHERE atom_id2 = 'TR000_2'
explanation: Both queries read from CONNECTED and select bond_id where atom_id2 = 'TR000_2'; the only difference is an alias in Q1, which does not affect semantics. They return the same multiset of bond_id values.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T.molecule_id FROM bond AS T WHERE T.bond_type = '=' ORDER BY T.molecule_id LIMIT 5
q2: SELECT T1.label FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.bond_type = ' = ' ORDER BY T1.label ASC LIMIT 5
explanation: Not equivalent. Q1 returns distinct molecule_ids from bonds whose bond_type is exactly '='. Q2 returns molecule labels for molecules having a bond whose bond_type is exactly ' = ' (with spaces), may include duplicates, and returns labels not ids. Different filter literal, selected column, and deduplication/order cause divergent results.
counterexample_dsp: Use one molecule with a bond_type '=' and another with bond_type ' = '. Q1 will return the first molecule_id; Q2 will return the second molecule's label.

q1: SELECT CAST(COUNT(CASE WHEN T.bond_type = '=' THEN T.bond_id ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T.bond_id) FROM bond AS T WHERE T.molecule_id = 'TR008'
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T1.bond_type = ' = ' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T1.bond_id) FROM bond AS T1 WHERE T1.molecule_id = 'TR008'
explanation: Both queries compute the percentage of bonds (for molecule TR008) whose bond_type matches a specific literal, but Q1 matches '=' while Q2 matches ' = ' (with spaces). Since VARCHAR preserves spaces in comparisons, the two predicates are different, so the queries are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Include bonds for molecule TR008 where some rows have bond_type '=' and others have bond_type ' = ' (with spaces). Q1 counts only the '=' rows; Q2 counts only the ' = ' rows, yielding different percentages.

q1: SELECT CAST(COUNT(CASE WHEN T.label = '+' THEN T.molecule_id ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T.molecule_id) FROM molecule t
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN label = '+' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(molecule_id) FROM molecule
explanation: Both compute 100 times the fraction of rows with label = '+'. In Q1 the numerator counts non-NULL molecule_id only when label = '+', which equals the number of '+' rows; in Q2 the numerator sums a 1/0 indicator for label = '+'. The denominator COUNT(molecule_id) equals total rows since molecule_id is NOT NULL (PK). They are equivalent for all non-empty tables; on an empty table, SUM yields NULL while COUNT yields 0, but both lead to a division-by-zero/NULL outcome depending on the DB.

q1: SELECT CAST(COUNT(CASE WHEN T.element = 'h' THEN T.atom_id ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T.atom_id) FROM atom AS T WHERE T.molecule_id = 'TR206'
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN element = 'h' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(atom_id) AS percentage FROM atom WHERE molecule_id = 'TR206'
explanation: Both compute the percentage of atoms that are 'h' within molecule TR206. They are aligned for non-empty inputs, but differ when there are no ATOM rows for TR206: COUNT(...) returns 0 while SUM(...) returns NULL. Thus Q1’s numerator is 0, Q2’s numerator is NULL, leading to different results on the empty input case.
counterexample: INSERT INTO MOLECULE (MOLECULE_ID) VALUES ('TR206');
counterexample_dsp: Have molecule TR206 present but no ATOM rows for it. Then Q1’s numerator is 0 while Q2’s numerator is NULL; the final expressions differ (Q1 evaluates 0.0*100/0; Q2 evaluates NULL*100/0, i.e., NULL).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T.bond_type FROM bond AS T WHERE T.molecule_id = 'TR000'
q2: SELECT T2.bond_type FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.molecule_id = 'TR000'
explanation: Q1 returns distinct bond_type values for bonds of TR000; Q2 joins to molecule and returns all matching bond_type rows without DISTINCT. If multiple bonds share the same bond_type for TR000, Q1 collapses duplicates while Q2 repeats them.
counterexample_dsp: Create molecule TR000 and insert two bonds for it with the same bond_type. Q1 returns one row; Q2 returns two rows.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T1.element, T2.label FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.molecule_id = 'TR060'

explanation: Q1 returns unique (element, label) pairs due to DISTINCT; Q2 returns all matching rows, including duplicates when a molecule has multiple atoms with the same element. The schema allows such duplicates.
counterexample_dsp: Molecule TR060 labeled 'Water' with two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Q2 outputs ('H','Water') twice; Q1 outputs it once.

q2: SELECT T1.bond_type FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.molecule_id = 'TR006' ORDER BY T1.bond_type ASC LIMIT 2
explanation: Q1 returns distinct bond_id values from CONNECTED edges whose atom_id belongs to molecule TR006 (without checking the bond’s molecule), while Q2 returns bond_type values of BOND rows whose molecule_id is TR006. q1: SELECT COUNT(T2.bond_id) FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id WHERE T1.molecule_id = 'TR009' AND T2.atom_id = T1.molecule_id || '_1' AND T2.atom_id2 = T1.molecule_id || '_2'
q2: SELECT COUNT(bond_id) FROM connected WHERE (atom_id = 'TR009_12' OR atom_id2 = 'TR009_12') AND bond_id LIKE 'TR009_%'
explanation: Q1 counts connections on bonds that belong to molecule TR009 and specifically connect TR009_1 to TR009_2 (in that order). Q2 counts connections whose bond_id string starts with 'TR009_' and where either endpoint equals TR009_12. They target different atom ids, Q1 is order-specific, and Q2 relies on a naming pattern instead of the bond’s molecule_id.

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T2.molecule_id) FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+' AND T1.element = 'br'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.molecule_id) FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN atom AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.label = '+' AND T2.element = 'br'
explanation: Both queries count the number of distinct molecules that (a) have label '+' and (b) have at least one atom with element 'br'. They perform the same inner join on molecule_id and apply the same predicates (label from MOLECULE, element from ATOM). Because the join enforces equality of molecule_id and MOLECULE.molecule_id is a PK (unique, non-null), COUNT(DISTINCT ...) over either side yields the same set. Hence they are semantically equivalent.

q2: SELECT T1.bond_type, T2.atom_id, T2.atom_id2 FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id WHERE T1.bond_id = 'TR001_6_9'
explanation: Both queries inner-join bond and connected on bond_id and then filter by the constant 'TR001_6_9'. Since the join enforces T1.bond_id = T2.bond_id, applying the filter on either side yields the same joined rows and the same projection. Primary key/foreign key constraints further ensure no mismatches; any rows with NULL bond_id in CONNECTED would neither join nor satisfy the WHERE in Q1.

q1: SELECT T2.molecule_id , IIF(T2.label = '+', 'YES', 'NO') AS flag_carcinogenic FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.atom_id = 'TR001_10'
q2: SELECT T2.label, CASE WHEN T2.label = '+' THEN 'Carcinogenic' ELSE 'Not Carcinogenic' END AS Carcinogenic FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.atom_id = 'TR001_10'
explanation: Both queries join the same tables and filter on the same atom, and both classify label = '+' as carcinogenic. However, Q1 projects molecule_id and a YES/NO flag, while Q2 projects the label and a different textual classification. Their outputs (columns and values) are not the same.

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T.molecule_id) FROM bond AS T WHERE T.bond_type = '#'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T1.molecule_id) FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.bond_type = '#'
explanation: Both queries count the number of distinct molecules that have at least one bond with bond_type '#'. Because BOND.molecule_id is a foreign key to MOLECULE, every qualifying bond row has a matching molecule, so the INNER JOIN in Q2 does not filter out any rows beyond the WHERE clause in Q1. COUNT(DISTINCT) ignores NULLs, and rows with NULL molecule_id would be excluded in both. Hence they are equivalent.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T.bond_id) FROM connected AS T WHERE SUBSTR(T.atom_id, -2) = '19'
q2: SELECT COUNT(bond_id) FROM connected WHERE atom_id LIKE 'TR%_19' OR atom_id2 LIKE 'TR%_19'
explanation: Q1 counts connections where atom_id ends with '19'. Q2 counts connections where either atom_id or atom_id2 matches the stricter pattern 'TR%_19' (starts with 'TR', has at least one character before the final '19'). Thus Q2 both checks atom_id2 and imposes a prefix and length constraint that Q1 does not.
counterexample_dsp: Create one connection where atom_id ends with '19' but does not start with 'TR'. Q1 counts it; Q2 does not.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T.element FROM atom AS T WHERE T.molecule_id = 'TR004'
q2: SELECT element FROM atom WHERE molecule_id = 'TR004'
explanation: Q1 returns distinct element values for molecule TR004, while Q2 returns all matching rows (including duplicates). Since the schema allows multiple atoms of the same element within a molecule, the queries can differ.
counterexample_dsp: Have two ATOM rows for molecule TR004 with the same ELEMENT 'H' but different ATOM_IDs. Q1 yields one 'H'; Q2 yields two 'H' rows.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T.molecule_id) FROM molecule AS T WHERE T.label = '-'
q2: SELECT COUNT(molecule_id) FROM molecule WHERE label = '-'
explanation: Both queries count rows in MOLECULE where LABEL = '-', counting MOLECULE_ID values. Because MOLECULE_ID is a PRIMARY KEY (thus NOT NULL), COUNT(molecule_id) equals COUNT(*) over the filtered rows. The alias in Q1 has no effect. Therefore, they are semantically identical.

q2: SELECT molecule_id FROM molecule WHERE label = '+' AND molecule_id IN (SELECT molecule_id FROM atom WHERE SUBSTRING(atom_id, 7, 2) BETWEEN 21 AND 25)
explanation: Q1 checks the last two characters of atom.atom_id as strings between '21' and '25', while Q2 checks characters at positions 7–8 of atom.atom_id interpreted numerically between 21 and 25. These are different conditions.

q1: SELECT CAST(COUNT( CASE WHEN T1.element = 'cl' THEN T1.element ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T1.element) FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+'

explanation: Both aim to compute the percentage of 'cl' atoms among atoms in '+' molecules. Numerators are equivalent counts of 'cl'. Denominators differ: Q1 divides by COUNT(T1.element) (ignores NULL elements), while Q2 divides by COUNT(T2.molecule_id) (counts all joined rows, including atoms with NULL element). If any atom.element is NULL, results diverge.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T.element FROM atom AS T WHERE T.molecule_id = 'TR001'
q2: SELECT T1.element FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.molecule_id = 'TR001'
explanation: Q1 returns distinct elements for molecule TR001, while Q2 returns all matching atom elements (with duplicates) via a join. The join is redundant due to the foreign key, but the lack of DISTINCT in Q2 makes the results differ when multiple atoms in TR001 share the same element.

q2: SELECT T1.molecule_id FROM bond AS T1 WHERE T1.bond_type = ' = '
explanation: Q1 returns distinct molecule_ids where bond_type is exactly '='. Q2 returns molecule_ids (not deduplicated) where bond_type is exactly ' = ' (with leading and trailing spaces). These filters differ, and Q1 also applies DISTINCT while Q2 does not.
counterexample_dsp: Provide one bond with bond_type '=' (no spaces) and another with bond_type ' = ' (with spaces). Q1 returns M1; Q2 returns M2.

q1: SELECT T1.element FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T1.atom_id = T2.atom_id WHERE T2.bond_id = 'TR005_16_26'

Q2 does the same but further restricts to a fixed whitelist of element symbols. Since ELEMENT is unconstrained, atoms may have elements outside that list, making Q2 a proper subset of Q1 in general.
counterexample_dsp: A bond TR005_16_26 connects an atom with element 'fe' (not in Q2’s whitelist). Q1 returns 'fe'; Q2 returns no rows.

q1: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T2.molecule_id) FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '-' AND T1.bond_type = '-'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT T2.molecule_id) FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.bond_type = '-' AND T2.label = '-'
explanation: Both queries inner-join bond to molecule on molecule_id, then filter rows where molecule.label = '-' and bond.bond_type = '-'. They count DISTINCT T2.molecule_id from the filtered join. The WHERE predicates are identical (just reordered), and AND is commutative, so the result sets and counts are the same.

q1: SELECT T2.label FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.bond_id = 'TR001_10_11'
q2: SELECT T1.label FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.bond_id = 'TR001_10_11'
explanation: Both queries fetch the label of the molecule associated with the bond 'TR001_10_11' by inner-joining bond and molecule on molecule_id and filtering by the same bond_id. With bond_id as a primary key and molecule_id as a foreign key to a unique molecule row, both return the same single label (or no row if the bond is absent).

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T1.bond_id, T2.label FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.bond_type = '#'
q2: SELECT bond.bond_id, molecule.label AS Carcinogenic FROM bond INNER JOIN molecule ON bond.molecule_id = molecule.molecule_id WHERE bond.bond_type = '#';
explanation: Both queries inner-join bond to molecule on the PK/FK (molecule_id), filter bond.bond_type = '#', and return one row per bond with its molecule label. Because bond_id is a primary key and molecule_id is a primary key in molecule (and bond.molecule_id references it), each bond matches at most one molecule and each (bond_id, label) pair is unique. Thus DISTINCT in Q1 is redundant, and the only difference is a column alias in Q2, which does not affect row semantics.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T1.element FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+' AND SUBSTR(T1.atom_id, -1) = '4' AND LENGTH(T1.atom_id) = 7

explanation: Q1 returns the distinct element names for atoms in '+' molecules where atom_id is exactly 7 chars and ends with '4'. Q2 returns element plus a count, restricted to a whitelist of elements, and only requires the 7th character to be '4' (allowing longer atom_ids). Hence different filters and projections.
counterexample_dsp: Create a '+' molecule with two atoms: (1) atom_id='ABCDEF4' (length 7, ends with '4') and element 'mg' (not in Q2's whitelist) — appears in Q1 but not Q2; (2) atom_id='ABCDEF4X' (length 8, 7th char is '4') and element 'c' — counted in Q2 but excluded by Q1's length=7.

q1: SELECT CAST(COUNT(CASE WHEN T.element = 'h' THEN T.atom_id ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) / COUNT(T.atom_id) FROM ( SELECT DISTINCT T1.atom_id, T1.element, T1.molecule_id, T2.label FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.molecule_id = 'TR006' ) AS T UNION ALL SELECT DISTINCT T3.label FROM ( SELECT DISTINCT T1.atom_id, T1.element, T1.molecule_id, T2.label FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.molecule_id = 'TR006' ) AS T3
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN element = 'h' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / COUNT(element), label FROM atom INNER JOIN molecule ON atom.molecule_id = molecule.molecule_id WHERE atom.molecule_id = 'TR006'
explanation: Q1 unions two different result sets into one column: a single scalar ratio and then the molecule label(s) as separate row(s). Q2 aims to return a single row with two columns: the ratio and the label. They also compute denominators differently (Q1 uses COUNT(atom_id), Q2 uses COUNT(element)), so NULL elements change the ratio in Q2 but not in Q1. Hence they are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: One molecule TR006 with three atoms, one of which has NULL element. Q1’s ratio = 1/3 (counts all atoms), Q2’s ratio = 1/2 (counts only non-NULL elements). Q1 also returns the label as a separate row via UNION ALL, unlike Q2 which returns it as a column.

explanation: Q1 lists the label of every molecule that has at least one atom with element = 'ca' (one row per matching atom, duplicates possible). Q2 returns a single Yes/No indicating whether there exists any molecule labeled '+' that has a 'ca' atom. They differ in scope (set vs single boolean), filtering (Q1 ignores label; Q2 requires label = '+'), and output shape.

INSERT INTO ATOM (atom_id, molecule_id, element) VALUES ('A1', 'M1', 'ca');

);

    FOREIGN KEY (atom_id2) REFERENCES atom(atom_id),

);

CREATE TABLE MOLECULE (
    MOLECULE_ID VARCHAR,

);
explanation: Q1 returns bond types from all bonds in any molecule that contains at least one 'te' atom (via molecule_id join), regardless of whether those bonds involve the 'te' atom. Q2 returns bond types only for bonds explicitly connected to a 'te' atom via the CONNECTED table (and could even span molecules since no FK enforces molecule consistency). Hence they are not equivalent.

explanation: Q1 returns the raw element code for only the atom stored in CONNECTED.atom_id for the given bond, while Q2 returns element names (via CASE mapping) for both atoms of the bond (matches on either CONNECTED.atom_id or CONNECTED.atom_id2). q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN bond.bond_type = '#' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(molecule.molecule_id) AS percentage FROM molecule LEFT JOIN bond ON molecule.molecule_id = bond.molecule_id
explanation: Q1 computes the percentage of bonds that are '#'. Q2 divides the number of '#' bonds by COUNT(molecule_id) over a LEFT JOIN, i.e., by (number of bonds + number of molecules with no bonds). They differ whenever at least one molecule has no bonds.

q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.bond_type = ' = ' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T2.bond_id) FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.molecule_id = 'TR047'
explanation: Both queries aim to compute the percentage of bonds of molecule TR047 that have bond_type equal to '='. However, Q2 compares bond_type to ' = ' (with spaces), while Q1 compares to '=' (no spaces). This makes them return different results when bond_type values do not include those spaces. The join vs. filter produces the same bond set due to the FK and PK constraints.
counterexample:

INSERT INTO BOND (bond_id, molecule_id, bond_type) VALUES ('b1', 'TR047', '=');

q2: SELECT CASE WHEN T1.label = '+' THEN 'Yes' ELSE 'No' END AS IsCarcinogenic FROM molecule AS T1 INNER JOIN atom AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.atom_id = 'TR001_1'
explanation: Q1 returns the molecule.label value for the atom, while Q2 maps label to a derived Yes/No based on whether label = '+'. They differ in output domain and in handling of any non-'+' (including NULL) labels.

q2: SELECT CASE WHEN label = '+' THEN 'Yes' ELSE 'No' END AS IsCarcinogenic FROM molecule WHERE molecule_id = 'TR151'
explanation: Q1 returns the raw LABEL value for molecule TR151, while Q2 maps LABEL to a derived Yes/No (only '+' becomes 'Yes', everything else including NULL becomes 'No'). Thus outputs differ whenever a row exists.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT T.element FROM atom AS T WHERE T.molecule_id = 'TR151'
q2: SELECT T1.element FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = 'TR151' AND T1.element IN ('cl', 'br', 'f', 'i', 'pb', 'te')
explanation: Q1 returns DISTINCT elements for atoms whose molecule_id equals 'TR151'. Q2 returns elements for atoms whose molecule’s LABEL equals 'TR151', restricted to a specific element set and without DISTINCT. They differ on id vs label filtering, element restriction, and deduplication.
counterexample_dsp: Create a molecule with id 'X1' but label 'TR151', and two atoms 'cl' in it. Q1 finds no rows (no atom has molecule_id='TR151'); Q2 finds two rows via the label match and allowed element list.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T.molecule_id) FROM molecule AS T WHERE T.label = '+'
q2: SELECT COUNT(molecule_id) FROM molecule WHERE label = '+'
explanation: Both queries count rows in MOLECULE where LABEL = '+'. Using an alias (T) or not does not change semantics, and COUNT(column) equals COUNT(*) here because MOLECULE_ID is a PRIMARY KEY (hence NOT NULL). Therefore, both return the same count.

q1: SELECT T.atom_id FROM atom AS T WHERE T.molecule_id BETWEEN 'TR010' AND 'TR050' AND T.element = 'c'
q2: SELECT atom_id FROM atom WHERE element = 'c' AND substr(molecule_id, 3, 3) BETWEEN 10 AND 50
explanation: Q1 keeps atoms with element 'c' whose full molecule_id string is lexicographically between 'TR010' and 'TR050'. Q2 keeps atoms with element 'c' whose characters 3–5, interpreted numerically, are between 10 and 50, regardless of prefix/suffix. Thus Q2 can include IDs not starting with 'TR' or with extra suffixes that Q1 excludes; also Q1 is lexicographic while Q2 is numeric.
counterexample_dsp: Molecules 'TS010' and 'TR050X' each have a 'c' atom. Q1 returns none (neither full ID lies in ['TR010','TR050']), while Q2 returns both (substr(...) = '010' -> 10 and '050' -> 50).

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.atom_id) FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+'
q2: SELECT COUNT(atom_id) FROM atom WHERE molecule_id IN (SELECT molecule_id FROM molecule WHERE label = '+')
explanation: Both queries count the number of atoms whose molecule has label '+'. Q1 does it via an inner join on molecule, Q2 via an IN subquery over molecule_ids with label '+'. Given molecule.molecule_id is a primary key (unique, non-null) and atom.atom_id is a non-null primary key (so COUNT(atom_id) equals row count), and the FK ensures atom.molecule_id matches existing molecules (NULLs, if any, are excluded by both predicates), the two queries are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT T1.bond_id FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+' AND T1.bond_type = '='
q2: SELECT bond_id FROM bond AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+' AND T1.bond_type = '='
explanation: Both queries inner-join bond to molecule on molecule_id, filter rows with molecule.label='+' and bond.bond_type='=', and project the same unambiguous column bond_id. The T1 qualifier in Q1 is redundant, so both return identical results.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T1.atom_id) AS atomnums_h FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.label = '+' AND T1.element = 'h'
q2: SELECT COUNT(atom_id) FROM atom WHERE molecule_id IN (SELECT molecule_id FROM molecule WHERE label = '+') AND element = 'H'
explanation: Both queries count atoms in molecules labeled '+', but Q1 filters ELEMENT = 'h' (lowercase) while Q2 filters ELEMENT = 'H' (uppercase). With case-sensitive string comparison (common in SQL systems like PostgreSQL), these are different, so the counts can diverge.
counterexample:

q2: SELECT CAST(COUNT(T1.ID) AS REAL) / 12 FROM Laboratory AS T1 INNER JOIN Patient AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T2.SEX = 'M' AND T1.Date BETWEEN '1998-01-01' AND '1998-12-31'
explanation: Both queries count male patients’ lab rows in 1998 and divide by 12, but they filter dates differently. Q1 uses strftime('%Y', Date)='1998' (year-based), while Q2 uses a string BETWEEN '1998-01-01' and '1998-12-31'. Rows with time components on 1998 dates (e.g., '1998-12-31 12:00:00') are included by Q1 but excluded by Q2 due to lexicographic string comparison. Also, Q2 may include invalid 1998-like strings that strftime would reject.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO PATIENT (ID, SEX) VALUES (1, 'M');
INSERT INTO LABORATORY (ID, DATE) VALUES (1, '1998-12-31 12:00:00');
counterexample_dsp: One male patient with a lab record on '1998-12-31 12:00:00'. Q1 includes it (year=1998). Q2 excludes it because the value is greater than the upper bound '1998-12-31' when compared as text.

q2: SELECT MAX(T2.Date), STRFTIME('%Y', T1.`First Date`) - STRFTIME('%Y', T1.Birthday) FROM Patient AS T1 INNER JOIN Laboratory AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.Diagnosis = 'SJS' ORDER BY T1.Birthday LIMIT 1

explanation: Q1 counts qualifying joined rows (one per qualifying lab record), while Q2 counts distinct patients with at least one qualifying lab record. They differ when a patient with Admission='-' has multiple lab rows with ALP<300 (or if Patient has duplicate rows for the same ID).
counterexample_dsp: One patient admitted as '-' has two lab tests with ALP<300. Q1 counts 2 rows; Q2 counts 1 distinct patient.

q2: SELECT T2.`aCL IgG`, T2.`aCL IgM`, T2.`aCL IgA` FROM Laboratory AS T1 INNER JOIN Examination AS T2 ON T1.ID = T2.ID WHERE T1.UA <= 7.2 AND T1.UA >= 3.7 AND T1.ID IN (SELECT ID FROM Patient WHERE SEX = 'F') ORDER BY T1.UA DESC LIMIT 1

Therefore COUNT(T2.link_to_event) = COUNT(T2.link_to_member) = COUNT(*) per event. Since EVENT_ID is the primary key of EVENT, EVENT_NAME is functionally dependent on it, making the SELECT valid.     PRIMARY KEY (budget_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (link_to_event) REFERENCES event(event_id)
);

explanation: Both join member to expense and filter for members with position 'Vice President', but Q1 projects (expense_id, expense_description) while Q2 projects only expense_description. Different projection means non-equivalence; if multiple expenses share a description, Q2 loses the ID distinction.
counterexample_dsp: One Vice President member with two expenses that share the same description. Q1 returns two distinct (expense_id, description) rows; Q2 returns two identical description rows and lacks the IDs.

q1: SELECT T2.date_received FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN income AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member WHERE T1.first_name = 'Casey' AND T1.last_name = 'Mason'
q2: SELECT T1.date_received FROM income AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.link_to_member = T2.member_id WHERE T2.first_name = 'Casey' AND T2.last_name = 'Mason'
explanation: Both queries perform the same inner join between MEMBER and INCOME on member_id = link_to_member, filter members where first_name = 'Casey' and last_name = 'Mason', and return the income.date_received. The only difference is alias naming; semantically they are identical.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T2.member_id) FROM zip_code AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.zip_code = T2.zip WHERE T1.state = 'Maryland'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT member_id) FROM member INNER JOIN zip_code ON member.zip = zip_code.zip_code WHERE zip_code.state = 'Maryland'
explanation: Both queries count members whose zip references a ZIP_CODE row with state='Maryland'. Because ZIP_CODE.zip_code is a primary key and MEMBER.zip is a foreign key to it, each member joins to exactly one ZIP_CODE row. MEMBER.member_id is a primary key (unique, non-null). Therefore COUNT(member_id) over the join equals COUNT(DISTINCT member_id), making Q1 and Q2 semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T2.department = 'School of Applied Sciences, Technology and Education'
q2: SELECT T2.first_name, T2.last_name FROM major AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.major_id = T2.link_to_major WHERE T1.department = 'School of Applied Sciences, Technology and Education'
explanation: Both queries perform the same inner join between MEMBER and MAJOR on MEMBER.link_to_major = MAJOR.major_id and filter by MAJOR.department = 'School of Applied Sciences, Technology and Education'. They then project the member’s first_name and last_name. Swapping join order and aliases does not change the result of an inner join, so the outputs are identical (including duplicates).

q1: SELECT T2.event_name FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T2.status = 'Closed' ORDER BY T1.spent / T1.amount DESC LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT T1.event_name FROM event AS T1 INNER JOIN budget AS T2 ON T1.event_id = T2.link_to_event WHERE T1.status = 'Closed' ORDER BY (T2.spent / T2.amount) DESC LIMIT 1
clean_ddl:
CREATE TABLE EVENT (
    EVENT_ID VARCHAR,
    EVENT_NAME VARCHAR,
    STATUS VARCHAR,
    PRIMARY KEY (event_id)
);

CREATE TABLE BUDGET (
    BUDGET_ID VARCHAR,
    SPENT REAL,
    AMOUNT INT,
    LINK_TO_EVENT VARCHAR,
    PRIMARY KEY (budget_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (link_to_event) REFERENCES event(event_id)
);
explanation: Both queries inner-join budget to event on link_to_event = event_id, filter to events with status = 'Closed', order rows by the budget ratio (spent/amount) in descending order, and return the event_name from the top-ranked row (LIMIT 1). The aliasing is swapped but the logic and returned value are the same. Any tie/non-determinism in ordering affects both identically.

q1: SELECT COUNT(member_id) FROM member WHERE position = 'President'
q2: SELECT COUNT(member_id) FROM member WHERE position = 'President'
explanation: Both queries are identical: they count the number of rows in MEMBER where POSITION = 'President'. Since MEMBER_ID is a PRIMARY KEY (thus NOT NULL), COUNT(member_id) equals COUNT(*) under the filter, making the results the same.

q1: SELECT MAX(spent) FROM budget
q2: SELECT T1.event_name FROM event AS T1 INNER JOIN budget AS T2 ON T1.event_id = T2.link_to_event ORDER BY T2.spent DESC LIMIT 1
explanation: Q1 returns the numeric maximum spent value from budget; Q2 returns the event_name of the event associated with the highest spent. They return different types and answer different questions. They also differ on empty input (Q1: NULL vs Q2: no rows) and tie-handling.
counterexample_dsp: Two events with budgets 100 and 200. Q1 returns 200, while Q2 returns the event name of the 200-spent budget (e.g., 'B').

q1: SELECT COUNT(event_id) FROM event WHERE type = 'Meeting' AND SUBSTR(event_date, 1, 4) = '2020'
q2: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM event WHERE type = 'Meeting' AND STRFTIME('%Y', event_date) = '2020'
explanation: Both count meetings in 2020, but Q1 checks the first 4 characters of EVENT_DATE, while Q2 extracts the year via STRFTIME, which parses and normalizes dates. Thus Q1 is purely textual; Q2 is calendar-aware and returns NULL for unparseable strings.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO EVENT (EVENT_ID, EVENT_DATE, TYPE) VALUES ('e1', '2020', 'Meeting');
INSERT INTO EVENT (EVENT_ID, EVENT_DATE, TYPE) VALUES ('e2', '2020-13-01', 'Meeting');
counterexample_dsp: EVENT rows where EVENT_DATE starts with '2020' but is not a valid/recognized date or normalizes to a different year. For example, '2020' (unparseable) or '2020-13-01' (normalizes to 2021). Q1 counts them; Q2 does not match year 2020.

q1: SELECT SUM(spent) FROM budget WHERE category = 'Food'
q2: SELECT SUM(spent) FROM budget WHERE category = 'Food'
explanation: Both queries identically compute SUM(spent) over rows in BUDGET where category = 'Food'. They have the same filter, same aggregation, and identical NULL behavior, so they are semantically equivalent on all databases under the given schema.

q1: SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN attendance AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member GROUP BY T2.link_to_member HAVING COUNT(T2.link_to_event) > 7
q2: SELECT first_name, last_name FROM member INNER JOIN attendance ON member.member_id = attendance.link_to_member GROUP BY member.member_id HAVING COUNT(attendance.link_to_event) > 7
explanation: Both queries return the names of members who have attended more than 7 events. They each inner-join member to attendance and form one group per member present in attendance: Q1 groups by attendance.link_to_member, Q2 by member.member_id. Because of the join equality (member.member_id = attendance.link_to_member) and the primary key on member.member_id, these groupings are identical. COUNT(attendance.link_to_event) counts non-null PK components, so both compute the same counts, and first_name/last_name are functionally determined by the grouped member id in both queries. Hence they are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT T2.first_name, T2.last_name FROM major AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.major_id = T2.link_to_major INNER JOIN attendance AS T3 ON T2.member_id = T3.link_to_member INNER JOIN event AS T4 ON T3.link_to_event = T4.event_id WHERE T4.event_name = 'Community Theater' AND T1.major_name = 'Interior Design'
q2: SELECT M.first_name, M.last_name FROM member AS M INNER JOIN major AS MJ ON M.link_to_major = MJ.major_id INNER JOIN attendance AS A ON M.member_id = A.link_to_member INNER JOIN event AS E ON A.link_to_event = E.event_id WHERE MJ.major_name = 'Interior Design' AND E.event_name = 'Community Theater'
explanation: Both queries inner-join major -> member -> attendance -> event via the same FK/PK keys, then filter for major_name = 'Interior Design' and event_name = 'Community Theater', and return the member’s first_name and last_name. The only differences are aliases and join order; with inner joins these are associative/commutative. Given the PKs (major_id, event_id, and attendance PK on (link_to_event, link_to_member)), no duplicate inflation arises. Therefore, Q1 and Q2 are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN zip_code AS T2 ON T1.zip = T2.zip_code WHERE T2.city = 'Georgetown' AND T2.state = 'South Carolina'
q2: SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN zip_code AS T2 ON T1.zip = T2.zip_code WHERE T2.city = 'Georgetown' AND T2.state = 'South Carolina'
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are identical: both return first and last names of members whose ZIP joins to a ZIP_CODE row with city = 'Georgetown' and state = 'South Carolina'. They use the same join and filters, so they are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT T2.amount FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN income AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member WHERE T1.first_name = 'Grant' AND T1.last_name = 'Gilmour'
q2: SELECT SUM(amount) FROM income AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.link_to_member = T2.member_id WHERE T2.first_name = 'Grant' AND T2.last_name = 'Gilmour'
explanation: Q1 returns one row per income.amount for members named 'Grant Gilmour'; Q2 returns a single row with the SUM of those amounts. Different cardinality and values (and Q1 can be empty while Q2 yields NULL on no matches).
counterexample_dsp: Member 'Grant Gilmour' has two income rows (100, 50). Q1 outputs two rows [100, 50]; Q2 outputs a single row [150].

q1: SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN income AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member WHERE T2.amount > 40
q2: SELECT T2.first_name, T2.last_name FROM income AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.link_to_member = T2.member_id WHERE T1.amount > 40
explanation: Both queries perform an inner join between MEMBER and INCOME on member_id = link_to_member, filter on INCOME.amount > 40, and project the MEMBER's first_name and last_name. They only differ in aliasing/join order, so they return identical results (including multiplicities).

q1: SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name, T2.source FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN income AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member GROUP BY T1.first_name, T1.last_name, T2.source ORDER BY SUM(T2.amount) DESC LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name, T2.source FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN income AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member ORDER BY T2.amount DESC LIMIT 1
explanation: Q1 returns the (member, source) group with the highest total income (SUM over all rows), while Q2 returns the single income row with the highest individual amount. Aggregation vs single-row selection makes them inequivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Member A has two 'Job' incomes 60+60=120; Member B has one 'Bonus' income 100. Q1 picks A/Job (total 120). Q2 picks B/Bonus (single 100).

q1: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN major_name = 'Finance' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / SUM(CASE WHEN major_name = 'Physics' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS ratio FROM major
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN major_name = 'Finance' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / SUM(CASE WHEN major_name = 'Physics' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM member INNER JOIN major ON member.link_to_major = major.major_id
explanation: Q1 computes (# of MAJOR rows named 'Finance') / (# of MAJOR rows named 'Physics'). Q2 computes (# of MEMBERs whose joined MAJOR is 'Finance') / (# of MEMBERs whose joined MAJOR is 'Physics'), and also forces floating-point division. Different grains (majors vs members) and join effects make them inequivalent.
counterexample_dsp: One Finance major and one Physics major. Three members: two in the Finance major and one in the Physics major. Q1 = 1/1 = 1. Q2 = 2/1 = 2.

q1: SELECT source FROM income WHERE date_received BETWEEN '2019-09-01' and '2019-09-30' ORDER BY source DESC LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT source FROM income WHERE date_received BETWEEN '2019-09-01' AND '2019-09-30' GROUP BY source ORDER BY SUM(amount) DESC LIMIT 1
explanation: Q1 returns the lexicographically greatest source among September 2019 rows, ignoring amounts. Q2 groups by source and returns the source with the highest total SUM(amount) in that month. These are different selection criteria.
counterexample_dsp: Create two September 2019 incomes: source 'Zeta' with a small amount and source 'Alpha' with a large amount. Q1 picks 'Zeta' (lexicographically greatest); Q2 picks 'Alpha' (largest total amount).

q1: SELECT first_name, last_name, email FROM member WHERE position = 'Secretary'
q2: SELECT first_name, last_name, email FROM member WHERE position = 'Secretary'
explanation: Both queries are identical: they select first_name, last_name, and email from MEMBER where position = 'Secretary'.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T2.member_id) FROM major AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.major_id = T2.link_to_major WHERE T1.major_name = 'Physics Teaching'
q2: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T2.major_name = 'Physics Teaching'
explanation: Both queries inner-join MEMBER to MAJOR on major_id and restrict to MAJOR.major_name = 'Physics Teaching'. Q1 counts T2.member_id, which is never NULL (PRIMARY KEY), so COUNT(T2.member_id) equals COUNT(*) in Q2. Hence they return the same count under the given schema.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T2.link_to_member) FROM event AS T1 INNER JOIN attendance AS T2 ON T1.event_id = T2.link_to_event WHERE T1.event_name = 'Community Theater' AND SUBSTR(T1.event_date, 1, 4) = '2019'
q2: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT link_to_member) FROM attendance AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T2.event_name = 'Community Theater' AND STRFTIME('%Y', T2.event_date) = '2019'
explanation: Both queries join event and attendance and filter for 'Community Theater' in 2019, but Q1 counts all attendance rows (COUNT of a non-null PK column) while Q2 counts distinct members. They can also diverge because Q1 uses SUBSTR(year) whereas Q2 uses STRFTIME(year) on a VARCHAR date. Hence not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: One member attends two different 'Community Theater' events in 2019. Q1 counts 2 rows; Q2 counts 1 distinct member.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T3.link_to_event), T1.major_name FROM major AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.major_id = T2.link_to_major INNER JOIN attendance AS T3 ON T2.member_id = T3.link_to_member WHERE T2.first_name = 'Luisa' AND T2.last_name = 'Guidi' group by T1.major_name
q2: SELECT COUNT(T1.link_to_event), T5.major_name FROM attendance AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.link_to_member = T2.member_id INNER JOIN major AS T5 ON T2.link_to_major = T5.major_id WHERE T2.first_name = 'Luisa' AND T2.last_name = 'Guidi'
explanation: Q1 groups by major_name and returns one row per major of members named 'Luisa Guidi', counting attendances per major. Q2 aggregates all matching rows into a single count (no GROUP BY) and also selects an unaggregated major_name, so it returns a single row (and is non-standard unless a lax SQL mode is used). They are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Two members both named 'Luisa Guidi' but in different majors and with different attendance counts. Q1 returns two rows (one per major). Q2 returns a single total count and an arbitrary major_name.

q1: SELECT SUM(spent) / COUNT(spent) FROM budget WHERE category = 'Food' AND event_status = 'Closed'
q2: SELECT AVG(T1.spent) FROM budget AS T1 WHERE T1.category = 'Food' AND T1.event_status = 'Closed'
explanation: Both queries compute the average of SPENT over rows where category='Food' and event_status='Closed'. Q1 does SUM(spent)/COUNT(spent); since both SUM and COUNT(column) ignore NULLs, this matches AVG(spent), which also ignores NULLs. When there are no non-NULL qualifying values, both yield NULL. Any differences would be limited to implementation-specific numeric precision, not semantics.

q1: SELECT T2.event_name FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T1.category = 'Advertisement' ORDER BY T1.spent DESC LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT T1.event_name FROM event AS T1 INNER JOIN budget AS T2 ON T1.event_id = T2.link_to_event WHERE T2.category = 'Advertisement' ORDER BY T2.spent DESC LIMIT 1
explanation: Both queries perform the same inner join between budget and event (budget.link_to_event = event.event_id), filter to budgets with category = 'Advertisement', order by the budget.spent in descending order, take the top row (LIMIT 1), and return the corresponding event_name. The differences are only alias names and join direction, which do not affect semantics. Any tie on spent is unresolved in both queries in the same way.

q1: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'Community Service' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(type) FROM event WHERE SUBSTR(event_date, 1, 4) = '2019'
q2: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'Community Service' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(event_id) FROM event WHERE event_date BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-12-31'
explanation: Both aim to compute the percentage of 2019 events that are 'Community Service', but Q1 filters by year prefix and divides by COUNT(type) (non-NULL types), while Q2 filters by a date range and divides by COUNT(event_id) (all rows). Differences in filtering and denominator make them inequivalent.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO EVENT (EVENT_ID, EVENT_DATE, TYPE) VALUES ('e1', '2019-05-01', 'Community Service');
INSERT INTO EVENT (EVENT_ID, EVENT_DATE, TYPE) VALUES ('e2', '2019-05-02', NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Two 2019 events: one with type 'Community Service', one with type NULL. Q1 divides by non-NULL types (1), Q2 divides by rows (2), yielding 100 vs 50.

q1: SELECT t_shirt_size FROM member GROUP BY t_shirt_size ORDER BY COUNT(t_shirt_size) DESC LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT t_shirt_size FROM member GROUP BY t_shirt_size ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 1
explanation: Both queries aim to return the most frequent t_shirt_size. Q1 orders by COUNT(t_shirt_size), which ignores NULLs, while Q2 orders by COUNT(*), which counts all rows (including those where t_shirt_size is NULL). They differ when there are members with NULL t_shirt_size: Q2 can select NULL as the most frequent size, but Q1 will never do so (it counts NULLs as 0).
counterexample_dsp: Make NULL the most frequent t_shirt_size: two members have NULL and one has 'M'. Q1 ignores NULLs and returns 'M'; Q2 counts NULLs and returns NULL.

q1: SELECT T2.event_name FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T2.event_id = T1.link_to_event WHERE T1.event_status = 'Closed' AND T1.remaining < 0 ORDER BY T1.remaining LIMIT 1
q2: SELECT T1.event_name FROM event AS T1 INNER JOIN budget AS T2 ON T1.event_id = T2.link_to_event WHERE T1.status = 'Closed' AND T2.remaining < 0 ORDER BY T2.remaining ASC LIMIT 1
clean_ddl:
CREATE TABLE EVENT (
    EVENT_ID VARCHAR,
    EVENT_NAME VARCHAR,
    STATUS VARCHAR,
    PRIMARY KEY (event_id)
);

CREATE TABLE BUDGET (
    BUDGET_ID VARCHAR,
    REMAINING REAL,
    EVENT_STATUS VARCHAR,
    LINK_TO_EVENT VARCHAR,
    PRIMARY KEY (budget_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (link_to_event) REFERENCES event(event_id)
);
explanation: Both queries pick the event name for the most negative budget, but Q1 filters by BUDGET.event_status='Closed' while Q2 filters by EVENT.status='Closed'. Since these columns are independent, the result sets can differ.
counterexample_dsp: Make one event whose EVENT.status is Open but its budget row has event_status Closed (negative remaining), and another event whose EVENT.status is Closed but its budget row has event_status Open (negative remaining). Q1 returns the first event; Q2 returns the second.

q1: SELECT SUM(T2.amount), T2.category FROM event AS T1 INNER JOIN budget AS T2 ON T1.event_id = T2.link_to_event WHERE T1.event_name = 'April Speaker' ORDER BY T2.amount
q2: SELECT T1.category, T1.amount FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T2.event_name = 'April Speaker' ORDER BY T1.amount ASC
explanation: Q1 aggregates all matching budget rows into a single sum (but also selects a non-aggregated category, which is nondeterministic in some DBMS), while Q2 returns each matching budget row with its own category and amount. They differ in aggregation level and output shape.
counterexample_dsp: Create one event named 'April Speaker' with two budget items. Q1 collapses them into one row with SUM=300 and an arbitrary category; Q2 returns two rows (Food,100) and (Travel,200).

q1: SELECT budget_id FROM budget WHERE category = 'Food' AND amount = ( SELECT MAX(amount) FROM budget )
q2: SELECT budget_id FROM budget WHERE category = 'Food' ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 1
explanation: Q1 returns Food rows whose amount equals the global max amount across all categories; Q2 returns exactly one Food row with the highest amount within Food (ignoring other categories and breaking ties arbitrarily). They differ when the global max is outside Food or when multiple Food rows tie at the top.
counterexample_dsp: Make the overall max amount belong to a non-Food row. Then Q1 returns no rows, while Q2 returns the top Food row.

q1: SELECT budget_id FROM budget WHERE category = 'Advertisement' ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 3
q2: SELECT budget_id FROM budget WHERE category = 'Advertising' ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 3
explanation: Both queries fetch up to 3 highest-amount budgets, but Q1 filters category = 'Advertisement' while Q2 filters category = 'Advertising'. Different filter literals make them inequivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Create one event, then insert one budget with category 'Advertisement' and another with 'Advertising'. Q1 returns the 'Advertisement' row; Q2 returns the 'Advertising' row.

q1: SELECT SUM(cost) FROM expense WHERE expense_description = 'Parking'
q2: SELECT SUM(T1.cost) FROM expense AS T1 WHERE T1.expense_description = 'Parking'
explanation: Both queries sum COST from EXPENSE where EXPENSE_DESCRIPTION = 'Parking'. Q2 only introduces a table alias (T1); filtering, aggregation, and NULL handling are identical, so results are the same in all cases.

q1: SELECT SUM(cost) FROM expense WHERE expense_date = '2019-08-20'
q2: SELECT SUM(cost) FROM expense WHERE expense_date = '2019-08-20'
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are textually identical: both compute SUM(cost) from EXPENSE where EXPENSE_DATE = '2019-08-20'. They will always return the same result (including NULL if no rows match).

q1: SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name, SUM(T2.cost) FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN expense AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member WHERE T1.member_id = 'rec4BLdZHS2Blfp4v' group by T1.first_name, T1.last_name
q2: SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name, SUM(T2.cost) AS total_cost FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN expense AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member WHERE T1.member_id = 'rec4BLdZHS2Blfp4v' GROUP BY T1.member_id
explanation: Both queries join member to expense, filter to the same single member_id (a primary key), and compute SUM(cost). For that fixed member, first_name and last_name are constant across joined rows, so grouping by names (Q1) or by member_id (Q2) produces the same single group (or no row if there are no expenses). The only difference is the alias on the SUM in Q2.

q1: SELECT T2.expense_description FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN expense AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member WHERE T1.first_name = 'Sacha' AND T1.last_name = 'Harrison'
q2: SELECT T2.expense_description FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN expense AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member WHERE T1.first_name = 'Sacha' AND T1.last_name = 'Harrison'
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are textually identical. Both inner-join MEMBER to EXPENSE on member_id=link_to_member, filter for first_name='Sacha' and last_name='Harrison', and return expense_description. They always produce the same result multiset.

q1: SELECT T2.expense_description FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN expense AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member WHERE T1.t_shirt_size = 'X-Large'
q2: SELECT DISTINCT T2.expense_description FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN expense AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member WHERE T1.t_shirt_size = 'X-Large'
explanation: Q1 returns all matching expense_description values (including duplicates) for expenses linked to X-Large members; Q2 adds DISTINCT, deduplicating descriptions. Since expense_description is not constrained to be unique, the queries can differ.
counterexample_dsp: A member with t_shirt_size = 'X-Large' has two expenses with the same expense_description ('Travel'). Q1 returns two rows 'Travel'; Q2 returns one row 'Travel'.

q1: SELECT T1.zip FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN expense AS T2 ON T1.member_id = T2.link_to_member WHERE T2.cost < 50
q2: SELECT T2.zip FROM expense AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.link_to_member = T2.member_id WHERE T1.cost < 50
explanation: Both queries inner-join member to expense on member_id = link_to_member, filter joined rows where cost < 50, and project the member.zip column. They differ only in table aliases and join order; the resulting join relation and projected column (member.zip) are identical, including duplicate multiplicities. Therefore, Q1 and Q2 are semantically equivalent.

q1: SELECT T1.major_name FROM major AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.major_id = T2.link_to_major WHERE T2.first_name = 'Phillip' AND T2.last_name = 'Cullen'
q2: SELECT T1.major_name FROM major AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.major_id = T2.link_to_major WHERE T2.first_name = 'Phillip' AND T2.last_name = 'Cullen'
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are textually identical: both inner join MAJOR to MEMBER on MAJOR_ID=LINK_TO_MAJOR, filter MEMBER rows where FIRST_NAME='Phillip' and LAST_NAME='Cullen', and return MAJOR_NAME. They will always produce the same result on any database matching the schema.

q1: SELECT T2.position FROM major AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.major_id = T2.link_to_major WHERE T1.major_name = 'Business'
q2: SELECT T1.position FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T2.major_name = 'Business'
explanation: Both queries inner-join MEMBER to MAJOR on MEMBER.link_to_major = MAJOR.major_id, filter rows where the joined MAJOR.major_name = 'Business', and project the member's position. The only difference is aliasing. Because major_id is a PK and link_to_major is an FK, each qualifying member appears at most once. Therefore, the outputs are identical.

q1: SELECT COUNT(T2.member_id) FROM major AS T1 INNER JOIN member AS T2 ON T1.major_id = T2.link_to_major WHERE T1.major_name = 'Business' AND T2.t_shirt_size = 'Medium'
q2: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM member AS T1 INNER JOIN major AS T2 ON T1.link_to_major = T2.major_id WHERE T2.major_name = 'Business' AND T1.t_shirt_size = 'Medium'
